```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5
)
library(ggplot2)
```

Entropy is estimated from counts across a cell's nearest neighbours. More
sequencing can raise this estimate even when the underlying biology is
unchanged. This vignette explains why that happens, how to detect it, how to
correct it, and when the data cannot identify the cause.

## Why depth inflates entropy

Shannon entropy depends on proportions. Multiplying all counts by the same
number does not change it. For example, `c(0, 5, 10)` and `c(0, 1, 2)` both
give the same value with the plug-in estimator.

Lower sequencing depth does not multiply every count by the same number. It
resamples the observed molecules. If three molecules are sampled without
replacement from `c(0, 5, 10)`, the number drawn from the second category has
a hypergeometric distribution. The following code enumerates every outcome.

```{r depth-example}
shannon_bits <- function(counts) {
  probabilities <- counts[counts > 0] / sum(counts)
  -sum(probabilities * log2(probabilities))
}

full_counts <- c(0, 5, 10)
scaled_counts <- c(0, 1, 2)
draws <- 3L
second_category <- 0:3

outcomes <- lapply(second_category, function(value) {
  c(0, value, draws - value)
})
probability <- vapply(second_category, function(value) {
  choose(5, value) * choose(10, draws - value) / choose(15, draws)
}, numeric(1))
entropy <- vapply(outcomes, shannon_bits, numeric(1))

example_table <- data.frame(
  outcome = vapply(
    outcomes,
    function(value) paste0("(", paste(value, collapse = ", "), ")"),
    character(1)
  ),
  probability = round(probability, 3),
  entropy_bits = round(entropy, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)

cat("Full depth entropy:", round(shannon_bits(full_counts), 3), "bits\n")
cat("Scaled entropy:", round(shannon_bits(scaled_counts), 3), "bits\n")
knitr::kable(example_table)

expected_entropy <- sum(probability * entropy)
cat("Expected entropy after downsampling:",
    round(expected_entropy, 3), "bits\n")
cat("Drop from sampling alone:",
    round(100 * (1 - expected_entropy / shannon_bits(full_counts))), "%\n")
```

The bars below show the probability of each outcome. Fill records its entropy.
The two zero-entropy outcomes together carry
`r round(100 * sum(probability[entropy == 0]))` percent of the probability.

```{r depth-outcome-plot, fig.height=3.8}
outcome_plot <- data.frame(
  outcome = factor(example_table$outcome, levels = example_table$outcome),
  probability = probability,
  entropy_bits = entropy
)

ggplot(outcome_plot, aes(x = outcome, y = probability, fill = entropy_bits)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * probability)),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#D9D9D9", high = "#54278F") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    x = "Downsampled outcome",
    y = "Probability",
    fill = "Entropy\n(bits)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Entropy is concave, so subsampling biases its estimate downward. Deeply
sequenced cells can therefore receive higher entropy for no biological reason.

The BUB estimator corrects much of this bias when the alphabet is observed. It
cannot correct a category that was never observed. Normalising or log
transforming does not solve this problem. Normalisation fixes the scale, not
the sampling.

## A simulation with known causes

We now simulate counts and let `run_entropy()` compute entropy from them. We do
not simulate entropy values. There are 2,000 cells, four clusters, and 400
genes. The three planted-effect clusters contain 300 cells each. The control
contains 1,100 cells, which gives a stable reference distribution.

Each cluster has a centre in a two-dimensional latent space. Cell coordinates
are Gaussian around that centre. These coordinates define the nearest
neighbours, so no PCA is needed.

All clusters start from a common gene probability vector. A different set of
25 genes is perturbed in each cluster. The fold changes are 14 for `technical`
and `both`, 1.2 for `biological`, and 19 for `control`. These stronger
cluster-specific programs keep the raw cluster elevations well separated.
Each cell then receives its own probability vector from a Dirichlet
distribution. A lower concentration gives wider cell-to-cell expression
spread.

Normal-depth clusters have a median library size of 200 counts. High-depth
clusters have a median of 300 counts, so the depth ratio is 1.5. Local depth
also changes smoothly along the first latent coordinate. This makes a cell's
own depth informative about the depth of its neighbours. The residual
log-depth standard deviation is 0.2 and the spatial coefficient is 0.9.

The Dirichlet concentrations are 200,000 for `technical` and `control`, 400
for `biological`, and 5,000 for `both`. The lower values plant biological
expression spread. The value for `both` is 40 times lower than the
narrow-spread value, but it is less extreme than the `biological` value.

```{r simulation}
library(Entropy)
library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(20260813L)

n_cells <- 2000L
n_genes <- 400L
cluster_levels <- c("technical", "biological", "both", "control")
cluster_sizes <- c(
  technical = 300L,
  biological = 300L,
  both = 300L,
  control = 1100L
)
cluster <- factor(
  rep(cluster_levels, times = cluster_sizes),
  levels = cluster_levels
)

centres <- rbind(
  technical = c(-6, -6),
  biological = c(6, -6),
  both = c(-6, 6),
  control = c(6, 6)
)
embedding_residual <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_cells * 2L, sd = 0.7),
  ncol = 2L
)
embedding <- centres[as.character(cluster), , drop = FALSE] +
  embedding_residual

common_probability <- rgamma(n_genes, shape = 100, rate = 100)
common_probability <- common_probability / sum(common_probability)
cluster_probability <- matrix(
  rep(common_probability, length(cluster_levels)),
  nrow = n_genes,
  dimnames = list(paste0("gene", seq_len(n_genes)), cluster_levels)
)

cluster_fold <- c(
  technical = 14,
  biological = 1.2,
  both = 14,
  control = 19
)

for (j in seq_along(cluster_levels)) {
  selected <- seq.int((j - 1L) * 25L + 1L, j * 25L)
  cluster_probability[selected, j] <-
    cluster_probability[selected, j] * cluster_fold[[cluster_levels[[j]]]]
  cluster_probability[, j] <- cluster_probability[, j] /
    sum(cluster_probability[, j])
}

high_depth <- cluster %in% c("technical", "both")
library_log_median <- log(ifelse(high_depth, 300, 200))
library_size <- round(exp(
  library_log_median +
    0.9 * embedding_residual[, 1L] +
    rnorm(n_cells, sd = 0.2)
))

concentration <- rep(200000, n_cells)
concentration[cluster == "biological"] <- 400
concentration[cluster == "both"] <- 5000

counts <- matrix(
  0L,
  nrow = n_genes,
  ncol = n_cells,
  dimnames = list(
    rownames(cluster_probability),
    paste0("cell", seq_len(n_cells))
  )
)

for (i in seq_len(n_cells)) {
  centre <- cluster_probability[, as.character(cluster[[i]])]
  probabilities <- rgamma(
    n_genes,
    shape = centre * concentration[[i]]
  )
  probabilities <- probabilities / sum(probabilities)
  counts[, i] <- as.vector(rmultinom(
    1L,
    size = library_size[[i]],
    prob = probabilities
  ))
}

rownames(embedding) <- colnames(counts)
colnames(embedding) <- c("latent_1", "latent_2")

simulated <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = Matrix::Matrix(counts, sparse = TRUE)
)
simulated$cluster <- cluster
simulated[["latent"]] <- CreateDimReducObject(
  embeddings = embedding,
  key = "LATENT_",
  assay = "RNA"
)

planted_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA) ~ cluster,
  data = simulated[[]],
  FUN = median
)
knitr::kable(
  planted_summary,
  col.names = c("Cluster", "Median library size", "Median nFeature")
)
```

The embedding defines four separated neighbourhood systems. The quality-control
plots show the planted depth and detection differences.

```{r simulation-embedding, fig.height=4.2}
embedding_plot <- data.frame(
  latent_1 = embedding[, 1L],
  latent_2 = embedding[, 2L],
  cluster = cluster
)

ggplot(embedding_plot, aes(x = latent_1, y = latent_2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 0.8) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Latent 1", y = "Latent 2", colour = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r simulation-qc-plots, fig.show='hold', out.width='49%', fig.width=4.2, fig.height=3.8}
simulation_qc <- simulated[[]]
simulation_qc$cluster <- factor(simulation_qc$cluster, levels = cluster_levels)

ggplot(simulation_qc, aes(x = cluster, y = nCount_RNA, fill = cluster)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.35, linewidth = 0.35) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Library size, log scale") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none")

ggplot(simulation_qc, aes(x = cluster, y = nFeature_RNA, fill = cluster)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.35, linewidth = 0.35) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Detected features") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none")
```

The `technical` cluster has high depth and narrow biological spread. The
`biological` cluster has normal depth and wide biological spread. The `both`
cluster has both causes. The `control` cluster has normal depth and narrow
spread. These roles let matching separate a technical elevation from one that
survives at equal detection.

## Run the diagnostic

We first compute uncorrected entropy. The latent coordinates are already stored
as a Seurat reduction, so `run_entropy()` can use them directly.

```{r run-uncorrected}
set.seed(20260814L)

uncorrected <- run_entropy(
  seu = simulated,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors_method = "auto",
  reduction = "latent",
  dims = 1:2,
  k = 15,
  mode = "counts",
  add_assay = FALSE,
  meta_name = "entropy_raw"
)
```

The diagnostic includes neighbourhood density automatically. We also provide
library size and detected feature count. Both are technical covariates, and the
appropriate intervention is count downsampling.

```{r diagnose-uncorrected}
technical_covariates <- uncorrected[[]][
  , c("nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA"),
  drop = FALSE
]

uncorrected_diagnostic <- entropy_diagnose(
  seu = uncorrected,
  entropy = uncorrected$entropy_raw,
  embedding = embedding,
  k = 15,
  group = "cluster",
  covariates = technical_covariates,
  covariate_type = c(
    nCount_RNA = "technical",
    nFeature_RNA = "technical"
  ),
  covariate_intervention = c(
    nCount_RNA = "downsample_counts",
    nFeature_RNA = "downsample_counts"
  ),
  n_bins = 10,
  min_bin_n = 15,
  verbose = FALSE
)

q1_table <- uncorrected_diagnostic$covariate_info[
  order(
    uncorrected_diagnostic$covariate_info$r_squared,
    decreasing = TRUE
  ),
  c("covariate", "type", "r_squared", "spearman_rho")
]
knitr::kable(q1_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Read this Q1 table first. The covariate with the largest R squared has the
strongest global relationship with entropy and deserves attention first. A
small value does not support a major global effect, although a cluster-specific
effect can still exist.

Q2 asks whether each cluster is elevated at all. The dashed line is the global
median entropy.

```{r entropy-cluster-boxplot, fig.height=4.2}
global_entropy_median <- median(uncorrected_diagnostic$cell_data$entropy)
uncorrected_plot_data <- uncorrected_diagnostic$cell_data
uncorrected_plot_data$cluster <- factor(
  uncorrected_plot_data$cluster,
  levels = cluster_levels
)

ggplot(
  uncorrected_plot_data,
  aes(x = cluster, y = entropy, fill = cluster)
) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.35, linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = global_entropy_median,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#444444"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Cluster",
    y = "Mean entropy",
    title = "Uncorrected entropy by cluster"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none")
```

The cluster table uses four flags with precise meanings:

* `not elevated`: the cluster does not have high entropy, so there is no
  elevation to explain.
* `cannot tell`: too few cells outside the cluster occupy the same covariate
  range, so there is no fair comparison group.
* `explained`: after matching the covariate, the cluster is no longer higher
  than other cells. The direction can also reverse.
* `not explained`: after matching the covariate, the cluster is still higher
  than other cells.

**Always read `retained` with the flag.** The flag records a threshold crossing.
`retained` records magnitude. It is the matched standardized difference divided
by the original standardized cluster elevation or deficit. A cluster can be
flagged `not explained` even when only one quarter of its original elevation
remains. In that case the covariate still accounts for three quarters of the
elevation.

A `retained` value above 1 means the matched difference is larger than the raw
elevation. This often happens when the raw elevation is small, so the ratio is
unstable. Treat `retained` as informative only when the cluster is clearly
elevated. A value below 0 means the direction reversed. After matching on the
covariate, the cluster sits below other cells. This is the strongest signature
of an artifact.

Also inspect `support`. It is the fraction of cluster cells that entered usable
matched bins. A flag below the support threshold is not a verdict. The default
threshold is stored in `uncorrected_diagnostic$thresholds$support_threshold`.

The first inline plot shows the flags and retained fractions. `NA` means that
the absolute standardized entropy difference was below the
`retained_min_delta` threshold of
`r sprintf("%.1f", uncorrected_diagnostic$thresholds$retained_min_delta)`, so
the fraction was not stable enough to report.

```{r flag-tile}
tile_data <- uncorrected_diagnostic$cluster_table
tile_data$cluster <- factor(tile_data$cluster, levels = cluster_levels)
tile_data$flag <- factor(
  tile_data$flag,
  levels = c("not elevated", "explained", "cannot tell", "not explained")
)
tile_data$covariate <- factor(
  tile_data$covariate,
  levels = c("mean_knn_dist", "nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA")
)
tile_data$retained_label <- ifelse(
  is.finite(tile_data$retained),
  sprintf("%.2f", tile_data$retained),
  "NA"
)
tile_data$label_colour <- ifelse(
  tile_data$flag %in% c("explained", "not explained"),
  "white",
  "black"
)

ggplot(tile_data, aes(x = covariate, y = cluster, fill = flag)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = retained_label, colour = label_colour),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "not elevated" = "grey80",
    "explained" = "#D55E00",
    "cannot tell" = "#F0E442",
    "not explained" = "#0072B2"
  ), drop = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(cluster_levels)) +
  labs(
    x = "Covariate",
    y = "Cluster",
    fill = "Flag",
    title = "Diagnostic flags",
    subtitle = "Numbers inside tiles are retained fractions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))
```

The next plot shows the relationship that the `nFeature_RNA` diagnostic is
testing.

The matched-bin plot is the heart of the method. Each point is one fair
comparison at similar detection. Points consistently above zero mean that the
cluster elevation survives matching. Unusable bins are omitted.

```{r matched-bin-plot, fig.height=5.2}
matched_bins <- uncorrected_diagnostic$bin_table[
  uncorrected_diagnostic$bin_table$covariate == "nFeature_RNA" &
    uncorrected_diagnostic$bin_table$usable,
]
matched_bins$cluster <- factor(matched_bins$cluster, levels = cluster_levels)

ggplot(matched_bins, aes(x = bin, y = diff, size = n_in)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#666666") +
  geom_point(colour = "#54278F", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~cluster, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(matched_bins$bin))) +
  labs(
    x = "Detection bin",
    y = "Median entropy difference",
    size = "Cluster cells"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The shaded region in each panel is the detection range covered by usable bins.
Points outside it did not contribute to the matched verdict.

```{r entropy-feature-scatter}
usable_ranges <- aggregate(
  cbind(bin_lower, bin_upper) ~ cluster,
  data = matched_bins,
  FUN = function(value) c(min = min(value), max = max(value))
)
usable_ranges <- data.frame(
  cluster = factor(usable_ranges$cluster, levels = cluster_levels),
  xmin = usable_ranges$bin_lower[, "min"],
  xmax = usable_ranges$bin_upper[, "max"]
)

ggplot(
  uncorrected_plot_data,
  aes(x = nFeature_RNA, y = entropy, colour = cluster)
) +
  geom_rect(
    data = usable_ranges,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#B3CDE3",
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~cluster, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Detected features per cell",
    y = "Mean entropy",
    colour = "Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

`entropy_diagnose_report()` writes the full multi-page PDF report. It is not
called here because this vignette keeps all output inline.

## Fix depth bias

The direct fix is to thin every sufficiently deep cell to a common count depth
before entropy is estimated. The neighbourhoods remain unchanged.

```{r run-corrected}
set.seed(20260815L)

corrected <- run_entropy(
  seu = simulated,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors_method = "auto",
  reduction = "latent",
  dims = 1:2,
  k = 15,
  mode = "counts",
  add_assay = FALSE,
  meta_name = "entropy_raw",
  depth_correct = TRUE,
  depth_quantile = 0.05
)
```

This call stores the corrected score as
`entropy_raw_depth_corrected`. We now repeat the same diagnostic.

```{r diagnose-corrected}
corrected_covariates <- corrected[[]][
  , c("nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA"),
  drop = FALSE
]

corrected_diagnostic <- entropy_diagnose(
  seu = corrected,
  entropy = corrected$entropy_raw_depth_corrected,
  embedding = embedding,
  k = 15,
  group = "cluster",
  covariates = corrected_covariates,
  covariate_type = c(
    nCount_RNA = "technical",
    nFeature_RNA = "technical"
  ),
  covariate_intervention = c(
    nCount_RNA = "downsample_counts",
    nFeature_RNA = "downsample_counts"
  ),
  n_bins = 10,
  min_bin_n = 15,
  verbose = FALSE
)

q1_before <- uncorrected_diagnostic$covariate_info[
  , c("covariate", "r_squared", "spearman_rho")
]
q1_after <- corrected_diagnostic$covariate_info[
  , c("covariate", "r_squared", "spearman_rho")
]
q1_comparison <- merge(
  q1_before,
  q1_after,
  by = "covariate",
  suffixes = c("_before", "_after"),
  sort = FALSE
)
q1_comparison <- q1_comparison[
  match(q1_before$covariate, q1_comparison$covariate),
]

knitr::kable(
  q1_comparison,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Covariate",
    "R squared before",
    "Spearman rho before",
    "R squared after",
    "Spearman rho after"
  ),
  caption = "Q1 global associations before and after depth correction.",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r q1-change-text, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
count_row <- q1_comparison[q1_comparison$covariate == "nCount_RNA", ]
feature_row <- q1_comparison[q1_comparison$covariate == "nFeature_RNA", ]
density_row <- q1_comparison[q1_comparison$covariate == "mean_knn_dist", ]
cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    "The global R squared for library size fell from %.3f to %.3f, a drop of ",
    "%.3f. For detected features it fell from %.3f to %.3f, a drop of %.3f. ",
    "These changes are the direct evidence that depth correction removed the ",
    "headline technical association.\n"
  ),
  count_row$r_squared_before,
  count_row$r_squared_after,
  count_row$r_squared_before - count_row$r_squared_after,
  feature_row$r_squared_before,
  feature_row$r_squared_after,
  feature_row$r_squared_before - feature_row$r_squared_after
))
```

```{r cluster-comparison-table}

before <- uncorrected_diagnostic$cluster_table[
  uncorrected_diagnostic$cluster_table$covariate == "nFeature_RNA",
]
after <- corrected_diagnostic$cluster_table[
  corrected_diagnostic$cluster_table$covariate == "nFeature_RNA",
]
before <- before[match(cluster_levels, before$cluster), ]
after <- after[match(cluster_levels, after$cluster), ]
technical_density_retained <- uncorrected_diagnostic$cluster_table$retained[
  uncorrected_diagnostic$cluster_table$cluster == "technical" &
    uncorrected_diagnostic$cluster_table$covariate == "mean_knn_dist"
]

comparison_table <- data.frame(
  cluster = cluster_levels,
  before_entropy_delta = before$entropy_delta_std,
  after_entropy_delta = after$entropy_delta_std,
  before_r_squared = before$within_r_squared,
  after_r_squared = after$within_r_squared,
  before_retained = before$retained,
  after_retained = after$retained,
  before_flag = before$flag,
  after_flag = after$flag,
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  comparison_table,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Cluster",
    "Entropy difference before",
    "Entropy difference after",
    "Within-cluster R squared before",
    "Within-cluster R squared after",
    "Before retained",
    "After retained",
    "Before flag",
    "After flag"
  ),
  caption = paste(
    "Q4 within-cluster fits and matched nFeature_RNA results.",
    "R squared columns are within-cluster values."
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The R squared values in this table are the within-cluster relationships between
entropy and `nFeature_RNA`. The `technical` elevation disappears after depth
correction. That elevation was an artifact. The `biological` cluster remains
elevated and `not explained`. Its planted expression spread survives. The
`both` cluster remains slightly elevated and is `not explained` after
correction. Its standardized elevation is below the retained threshold of
`r sprintf("%.1f", corrected_diagnostic$thresholds$retained_min_delta)`, so
its retained fraction is `NA`. This marginal result should not be read as a
stable effect fraction.

The raw `retained` value for `technical` is
`r sprintf("%.3f", before$retained[before$cluster == "technical"])`. The
cluster looked elevated before matching, but that elevation is gone after
matching on detection. The small negative value means that it sits only
marginally below comparable cells. This is what a technical artifact looks
like, although the reversal itself is modest. The same cluster gives a clearer
example against `mean_knn_dist`, where its retained value is
`r sprintf("%.2f", technical_density_retained)`.

The same result is visible in the before and after distributions. The
`technical` elevation collapses, while the `biological` distribution remains
high.

```{r before-after-boxplots, fig.height=4.5}
before_after_entropy <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    cluster = uncorrected_diagnostic$cell_data$cluster,
    entropy = uncorrected_diagnostic$cell_data$entropy,
    stage = "Before correction"
  ),
  data.frame(
    cluster = corrected_diagnostic$cell_data$cluster,
    entropy = corrected_diagnostic$cell_data$entropy,
    stage = "After correction"
  )
)
before_after_entropy$cluster <- factor(
  before_after_entropy$cluster,
  levels = cluster_levels
)
before_after_entropy$stage <- factor(
  before_after_entropy$stage,
  levels = c("Before correction", "After correction")
)

ggplot(before_after_entropy, aes(x = cluster, y = entropy, fill = cluster)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.3, linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~stage) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean entropy") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none")
```

After correction, the entropy and detection relationship is much flatter. The
shaded range again marks usable matched bins.

```{r corrected-entropy-feature-scatter}
corrected_bins <- corrected_diagnostic$bin_table[
  corrected_diagnostic$bin_table$covariate == "nFeature_RNA" &
    corrected_diagnostic$bin_table$usable,
]
corrected_ranges <- aggregate(
  cbind(bin_lower, bin_upper) ~ cluster,
  data = corrected_bins,
  FUN = function(value) c(min = min(value), max = max(value))
)
corrected_ranges <- data.frame(
  cluster = factor(corrected_ranges$cluster, levels = cluster_levels),
  xmin = corrected_ranges$bin_lower[, "min"],
  xmax = corrected_ranges$bin_upper[, "max"]
)
corrected_plot_data <- corrected_diagnostic$cell_data
corrected_plot_data$cluster <- factor(
  corrected_plot_data$cluster,
  levels = cluster_levels
)

ggplot(
  corrected_plot_data,
  aes(x = nFeature_RNA, y = entropy, colour = cluster)
) +
  geom_rect(
    data = corrected_ranges,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#B3CDE3",
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~cluster, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Detected features per cell", y = "Depth-corrected mean entropy") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Downsampling works because it equalises how much each cell was sampled.
Normalisation only rescales numbers that were already sampled unequally.

`depth_quantile = 0.05` sets the target to the fifth percentile of library
sizes. It is therefore close to the fraction of cells left uncorrected. Cells
already below the target keep their original counts.

## What the diagnostic cannot do

The `both` cluster has two independent causes at once. High depth creates a
technical entropy effect, while wide expression spread creates a biological
effect. The observational diagnostic cannot separate those causes from the
scatter alone. The intervention can: downsampling removes the depth component,
and the remaining elevation is flagged `not explained`. This is why the before
and after results for `both` differ.

This simulation does not demonstrate the harder mediator problem. In real
data, progenitor cells may express more genes precisely because they are
multipotent. Detection is then part of the biological state rather than an
independent technical cause. Correcting for detection could remove real
biology. A simulation cannot demonstrate this ambiguity because its true causes
are always known by construction.

```{r both-cluster-highlight, fig.height=4.2}
both_cells <- uncorrected_plot_data$cluster == "both"

ggplot(uncorrected_plot_data, aes(x = nFeature_RNA, y = entropy)) +
  geom_point(
    data = uncorrected_plot_data[!both_cells, ],
    colour = "#C7C7C7",
    alpha = 0.3,
    size = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = uncorrected_plot_data[both_cells, ],
    colour = "#54278F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = uncorrected_plot_data[both_cells, ],
    colour = "#54278F",
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Detected features per cell",
    y = "Mean entropy",
    title = "The both cluster contains technical and biological effects"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

A flag of `explained` does not prove that a cluster is uninteresting. A flag of
`not explained` does not prove plasticity. These are screening results, not
conclusions.

`entropy_recompute_check()` provides stronger evidence than a statistical
adjustment because it changes the input and recomputes entropy. It supports
three mechanisms: `downsample_counts`, `subsample_cells`, and `remove_genes`.
It is not run here because it is slower. A dedicated vignette covers that
workflow.

## Decision guide

1. Run `entropy_diagnose()` and read the Q1 table first.
2. If `nFeature_RNA` or `nCount_RNA` has a large R squared, rerun
   `run_entropy()` with `depth_correct = TRUE`. This is the recommended default
   action.
3. Density has a small but non-zero effect in this simulation. The
   `mean_knn_dist` R squared is
   `r sprintf("%.3f", density_row$r_squared_before)` before correction and
   `r sprintf("%.3f", density_row$r_squared_after)` after correction, while
   Spearman rho changes from
   `r sprintf("%.3f", density_row$spearman_rho_before)` to
   `r sprintf("%.3f", density_row$spearman_rho_after)`. In data where density
   is large, use `subsample_cells` in `entropy_recompute_check()`.
4. If a gene score such as cell cycle is large, use `remove_genes`.
5. Always read `retained` with the flag. Never quote a verdict when `support`
   is below the threshold.

The practical default is simple. Diagnose first. Correct depth when count depth
or detected features dominate Q1. Then rerun the diagnostic and keep biological
claims separate from the screening flags.
